content: The protein known as Vasoactive Intestinal Polypeptide Receptor 1 (VIPR1), also referred to as VPAC1, is encoded by the VIPR1 gene in humans. VPAC1 is expressed in various tissues and organs, including the cerebral cortex, hippocampus, and amygdala of the brain, as well as the lung, prostate, peripheral blood leukocytes, liver, small intestine, heart, spleen, placenta, kidney, thymus, and testis. VPAC1 functions as a receptor for vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP), which is a small neuropeptide. VIP plays a role in several physiological processes, including the relaxation of smooth muscle, the regulation of exocrine and endocrine secretions, and the modulation of water and ion transport in the epithelial cells of the lung and intestine. The actions of VIP are mediated through integral membrane receptors that are coupled to guanine nucleotide-binding proteins (G-proteins), which subsequently activate adenylate cyclase. VIP also exerts autocrine effects via VPAC1 to inhibit the proliferation of megakaryocytes and promote the formation of proplatelets. In terms of clinical significance, patients with idiopathic achalasia exhibit notable differences in the distribution of single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) that affect the VIPR1 gene. Additionally, levels of VIP and pituitary adenylate cyclase-activating polypeptide (PACAP) are reduced in the anterior vaginal wall of patients with stress urinary incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse. These reductions may contribute to the pathophysiology of these conditions.
